vacant

VAY-kunt — stress on first syllable, the 'ay' sound rhymes with 'say' and 'way' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Vacant describes something empty or not occupied by anyone.

The vacant house on the corner finally sold after two years.

Example

The old mansion stood vacant for years, its windows dark and empty, waiting for owners who never came.

Vacant is more precise than 'empty' because it doesn't just mean nothing is inside—it emphasizes that a space meant to be inhabited by people is without occupants. The building's waiting, its abandonment, is central to what vacant means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bare: Bare means stripped of any covering or contents — bare walls hold no pictures, bare shelves no books. Vacant is not about what a surface holds; it says a space meant for people has no one in it. A vacant office can still be fully furnished, carpet to ceiling.

unused: Unused means nothing and no one is putting a thing to use, and it may never have been used at all. Vacant makes a narrower claim about a space meant for people: no one is occupying it. A brand-new house is unused; once its owners move out, it stands vacant.

available: Available means free to be taken, booked, or moved into — it points at what could happen next. Vacant only reports the present fact that no one is in the space. A vacant apartment already leased for next month is not available, even though it stands empty today.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

occupied: filled or in use by someone

inhabited: having people living inside it

Where it sits · how completely and permanently people are gone

unoccupied → empty → vacant → abandoned

unoccupied vs. vacant: Unoccupied is milder than vacant — an unoccupied seat simply has no one in it right now, while vacant suggests a place standing empty with no one there at all.

empty vs. vacant: Empty is slightly weaker than vacant; empty just means nothing is inside, while vacant adds the sense that a place meant to be used or lived in has no one in it.

abandoned vs. vacant: Abandoned is stronger than vacant — a vacant building merely has no occupants, but an abandoned one has been deserted for good, with no plan for anyone to return.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vac: empty, unoccupied (from vacāre, 'to be empty') (Latin)

Suffix — -ant: being in a state of; forms adjectives (Latin)

Put it together: The root vac- means 'empty,' and the suffix -ant turns it into a describing word — so vacant literally means 'being empty,' exactly what it still describes: a space with no one and nothing in it.

Use the root in a new word: evacuate: During the fire drill, the whole school practiced how to evacuate in under four minutes.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Use vacant when describing a space (house, office, lot, building) that is unoccupied and available. The word has a more definitive, property-related feel than empty in formal, real-estate contexts. For everyday situations where something just has nothing inside, 'empty' is simpler.
